newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela cuts forex band depreciation rate.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela cuts forex band depreciation rate.

text.p: Venezuela's Central Bank announced Monday that it had reduced the monthly depreciation rate for its foreign exchange bands system to 1.16 percent from 1.32 percent.

"In view of the effect that currency demand could be placing on expectations of an accelerated depreciation of the nominal exchange rate...the board of directors in a July 31 meeting decided to reduce the monthly rate (of depreciation) to 1.16 percent," the Bank said in a release.
The Bank said the alteration of the depreciation rate was justified "by the positive evolution of macro-economic variables and the reduction of the inflation rate."

Soon after abandoning currency controls in April 1996 the Central Bank established a currency bands system with the exchange rate allowed to fluctuate freely up to 7.5 percent either side of a sliding central rate.
Since Jan 1, 1997, the central rate has depreciated at 1.32 percent per month, in line with the government's projected inflation goal at the time of 25 percent for 1997.
However, the bolivar depreciated just 2.5 percent over the first half of the year as the Central Bank used the exchange rate as an anchor with which to reign in inflation.
But high levels of liquidity, low interest rates and an apparently less aggressive currency defense by the Central Bank saw the bolivar depreciate by two percent in July.

The high dollar demand "suggests the presence of speculative pressures which could have their origins in temporary excess liquidity levels and perhaps in unfounded exchange rate depreciation expectations," the Bank release said.

The Central Bank stressed that Venezuela's strong balance of payments and high level of foreign reserves, which stood at $16.6 billion at the end of July, meant that it could comfortably meet market needs and "neutralize speculative pressures."
"There is no reason to sustain depreciation expectations or create an unwanted overvaluation of the currency," it said.
Analysts have said that based on the rate of depreciation of the bolivar over recent weeks the exchange rate should end the year around 525 bolivars per dollar.
The bolivar closed sharply firmer at 494.50/495.50 bolivars per dollar Monday.
The announcement of a new exchange bands depreciation rate coincided with two related measures Monday.

The Central Bank raised commercial banks' reserve requirement two percentage points to 17 percent to drain excess liquidity which has been placing pressure on the bolivar. The new reserve requirement comes into effect Aug 11.
The Bank also introduced new limits on interbank foreign exchange trading, reclassifying a number of brokerages and institutions previously considered as end clients.
The two moves were designed to reduce currency trading volume and volatility and exert greater control on the market, traders and analysts said.
